claim: The gene regulatory network (GRN) is the central decision‐making module of the cell.
source: The gene regulatory network (GRN) is the central decision‐making module of the cell.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the role of GRNs in cellular function.

claim: GRNs are organised so that they remain robust in the face of unpredictable environmental and evolutionary changes.
source: We have developed a theory called Buffered Qualitative Stability (BQS) based on the hypothesis that GRNs are organised so that they remain robust in the face of unpredictable environmental and evolutionary changes.
evidence: This is the central hypothesis of the BQS theory presented in the manuscript.

claim: The GRNs of E. coli, M. tuberculosis, P. aeruginosa, yeast, mouse, and human all verify the predictions of BQS.
source: We show that the GRNs of E. coli, M. tuberculosis, P. aeruginosa, yeast, mouse, and human all verify the predictions of BQS.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis presented throughout the manuscript comparing real GRNs to random networks.

claim: BQS explains many of the small- and large‐scale properties of GRNs.
source: BQS explains many of the small- and large‐scale properties of GRNs, provides conditions for evolvable robustness, and highlights general features of transcriptional response.
evidence: This is supported by the various analyses of network properties at different scales presented in the manuscript.

claim: BQS is severely compromised in a human cancer cell line.
source: BQS is severely compromised in a human cancer cell line, suggesting that loss of BQS might underlie the phenotypic plasticity of cancer cells, and highlighting a possible sequence of GRN alterations concomitant with cancer initiation.
evidence: This is supported by data comparing the K562 cancer cell line to the GM12878 non-cancer cell line.

claim: Loss of BQS might underlie the phenotypic plasticity of cancer cells.
source: BQS is severely compromised in a human cancer cell line, suggesting that loss of BQS might underlie the phenotypic plasticity of cancer cells, and highlighting a possible sequence of GRN alterations concomitant with cancer initiation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed differences in BQS between cancer and non-cancer cell lines.

claim: Robustness is a remarkable feature of living organisms allowing them to tolerate a wide variety of contingencies.
source: Robustness is a remarkable feature of living organisms allowing them to tolerate a wide variety of contingencies, such as DNA damage, limitations in nutrient availability, or exposure to toxins (Lopez-Maury et al., 2008; MacNeil and Walhout, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on biological robustness.

claim: The robustness of a biological system should depend on qualitative, not quantitative, features of its response to perturbation.
source: We propose that the robustness of a biological system should therefore depend on qualitative, not quantitative, features of its response to perturbation.
evidence: This is a theoretical proposition that forms the basis of the BQS framework.

claim: Qualitative Stability has been studied before and applied to economics, ecology and chemistry.
source: This type of robustness has been studied before (Quirk and Ruppert, 1965; Puccia and Levins, 1985) and has been applied to economics (Quirk and Ruppert, 1965; Hale et al., 1999), ecology (May, 1973a; Puccia and Levins, 1985) and chemistry (Tyson, 1975).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on qualitative stability in other fields.

claim: Qualitative Stability has never been used to predict network features beyond simple topological properties or applied to molecular cell biology.
source: However, this notion has never been used to predict network features beyond simple topological properties required by the 'rules' that allow such stringent robustness and has not previously been applied to molecular cell biology, or the evolutionary pressures shaping the behaviours of living organisms.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the current work based on review of previous literature.

claim: Transcriptional regulation plays a central role in the behaviour of cells in response to environmental cues and is aberrant in many diseases.
source: Transcriptional regulation plays a central role in the behaviour of cells in response to environmental cues and is aberrant in many diseases (Lee and Young, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature on transcriptional regulation.

claim: Networks representing transcriptional interactions have been derived for diverse organisms.
source: Moreover, networks representing transcriptional interactions have been derived for diverse organisms.
evidence: This is supported by the availability of GRN datasets cited throughout the manuscript.

claim: A primary requirement for Qualitative Stability is the absence of long feedback loops.
source: A primary requirement for Qualitative Stability is the absence of long feedback loops (meaning, in the case of GRNs, feedback loops involving three or more genes) regardless of whether the connections comprising the loops are stimulatory or inhibitory.
evidence: This is a theoretical requirement derived from the mathematical theory of Qualitative Stability.

claim: The danger inherent in feedback loops was first analysed by James Clerk Maxwell who showed that mechanical governors regulating the output of steam engines can fail if the input changes faster than the system response.
source: The danger inherent in feedback loops was first analysed by James Clerk Maxwell who showed that mechanical governors regulating the output of steam engines can fail if the input changes faster than the system response, causing 'an oscillating and jerking motion, increasing in violence till it reaches the limit of action of the governor' (Maxwell, 1868).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Maxwell's historical work on feedback systems.

claim: The repressilator, a gene circuit consisting of a 3-gene feedback loop, produces oscillations of increasing intensity in vivo.
source: This concept is supported by the behaviour of the repressilator, a well-known gene circuit consisting of a 3-gene feedback loop, which has been shown to produce oscillations of increasing intensity in vivo (Elowitz and Leibler, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to experimental work on the repressilator.

claim: P. aeruginosa, S. cerevisiae and human GRNs have no feedback loops comprising three or more genes.
source: On studying feedback loops in the GRNs of these organisms (Figure 2A–C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B, lightly shaded bars), we find that P. aeurginosa, S. cerevisiae and human GRNs have no feedback loops comprising three or more genes.
evidence: This is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 2 and its supplements.

claim: The E. coli GRN has no feedback loops comprising four or more genes, and only two 3-gene feedback loops.
source: The E. coli GRN has no feedback loops comprising four or more genes, and only two 3-gene feedback loops.
evidence: This is supported by data analysis of the E. coli GRN.

claim: M. tuberculosis has two 3-gene feedback loops and one 4-gene feedback loop.
source: M. tuberculosis has two 3-gene feedback loops and one 4-gene feedback loop.
evidence: This is supported by data analysis of the M. tuberculosis GRN.

claim: All the 3-gene feedback loops observed in real GRNs share the same peculiar structure.
source: Notably, all the 3-gene feedback loops observed in real GRNs share the same peculiar structure, with implications discussed below.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis that is discussed further in the manuscript.

claim: Random networks of the size and connectivity of biological GRNs display an exponential increase in feedback loops consisting of three or more genes, numbering in the thousands.
source: In contrast, when networks of the size and connectivity of the biological GRNs are constructed with randomly placed links, they display an exponential increase in feedback loops consisting of three or more genes, which number in the thousands (Figure 2A–C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B, heavily shaded bars, and Figure 2—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is supported by computational simulations of random networks shown in Figure 2 and supplements.

claim: Each of 1000 randomly simulated E. coli networks had at least one long feedback loop.
source: Each of 1000 randomly simulated E. coli networks had at least one long feedback loop.
evidence: This is a result from computational simulations of random networks.

claim: There is an extremely small probability (<10−6) that the absence of long feedback loops with >3 genes in E. coli is a chance event.
source: Statistical analyses suggest that there is an extremely small probability (<10−6) that the absence of long feedback loops with >3 genes in E. coli is a chance event (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Similar statistical results hold for S. cerevisiae and human GRNs.
source: Similar results hold for S. cerevisiae (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B) and human (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B and 2C.

claim: The results on feedback loops are robust to variations in the confidence levels of the E. coli and S. cerevisiae GRNs.
source: These results are robust to variations in the confidence levels of the E. coli and S. cerevisiae GRNs (Figure 2—figure supplement 3E,J), despite large variations in other properties of the GRNs (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–D,F–I), and remain valid when different random models are considered (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is supported by sensitivity analyses shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and 4.

claim: Qualitative Stability of GRNs prevents the catastrophe described by Maxwell from occurring, even when any of the myriad quantitative system parameters are altered.
source: Qualitative Stability of GRNs prevents the catastrophe described by Maxwell from occurring, even when any of the myriad quantitative system parameters (TF abundance, promoter availability, the rate of transcription, etc.) are altered.
evidence: This is an inference based on the theory of Qualitative Stability and the observed properties of GRNs.

claim: The damped oscillatory response expected from a stable system has been observed in single cell experiments.
source: Notably, the damped oscillatory response expected from a stable system has been observed in single cell experiments (Tay et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to experimental work on single cell dynamics.

claim: A long feedback loop can be created by the addition of a feedback connection from a TF lower down in a network path to a TF higher up in that path.
source: For example, a long feedback loop can be created by the addition of a feedback connection from a TF lower down in a network path to a TF higher up in that path.
evidence: This is a logical inference about how network structure can be altered.

claim: The abundance of incomplete feedback loops in the GRNs of E. coli, S. cerevisiae and human is much lower than in comparable random networks.
source: The abundance of incomplete feedback loops in the GRNs of E. coli, S. cerevisiae and human is shown in Figure 3A–C (lightly shaded bars). Data for M. tuberculosis and P. aeruginosa are shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B. For each of these GRNs there are <2000 incomplete feedback loops and they tend to be of a relatively small size. A similar empirical observation has been made regarding transcriptional cascades (Rosenfeld and Alon, 2003; The modENCODE Consortium et al., 2010). This is in stark contrast to comparable random networks (Figure 3A–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B, heavily shaded bars, and Figure 3—figure supplement 4), which on average have a thousand-fold greater number of incomplete feedback loops (>105) of a significantly larger size.
evidence: This is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 3 and its supplements.

claim: There is an extremely small probability (<10−19) that the absence of long incomplete feedback loops is a chance event in E. coli, S. cerevisiae, and human.
source: Statistical analyses suggest that there is an extremely small probability (<10−19) that the absence of long incomplete feedback loops is a chance event in the three organisms considered (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The results on incomplete feedback loops are relatively robust to variations in the confidence levels of the E. coli and S. cerevisiae GRN.
source: These results are relatively robust to variations in the confidence levels of the E. coli and S. cerevisiae GRN (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A,B), and remain valid when different random models are considered (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by sensitivity analyses shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 and 4.

claim: The percentage of unregulated TFs in E. coli, S. cerevisiae, M. tuberculosis, P. aeruginosa, human and other yeast datasets is very high.
source: Consistent with this prediction, the percentage of unregulated TFs in E. coli, S. cerevisiae, M. tuberculosis, P. aeruginosa, human and other yeast datasets is very high (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: This is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 4 and its supplements.

claim: The probability of obtaining the observed proportion of unregulated TFs by chance is between 10−68 and 10−39.
source: Comparison with random networks indicates that the probability of obtaining this proportion of unregulated TFs by chance is between 10−68 and 10−39 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The results on unregulated TFs are robust to variations in the confidence levels of the E. coli and S. cerevisiae GRNs.
source: These results are robust to variations in the confidence levels of the E. coli and S. cerevisiae GRNs (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A,B), and remain valid when different random models are considered (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is supported by sensitivity analyses shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4 and Figure 2—figure supplement 4A.

claim: In E. coli, the TF with the largest number of outgoing regulatory connections regulates 38 other TF genes, but is itself regulated by only one TF.
source: The E. coli TF with the largest number of 'outgoing regulatory connections' regulates 38 other TF genes, but is itself regulated by only one TF; the TF with the largest number of 'incoming regulatory connections' is regulated by nine other TFs but itself regulates only one TF gene.
evidence: This is a specific observation from the E. coli GRN data analysis.

claim: There are no E. coli TFs that are both highly regulated and highly regulating.
source: There are no E. coli TFs that are both highly regulated and highly regulating (in fact, there are no TFs regulating >2 other TFs that are themselves regulated by >2 TFs).
evidence: This is a specific observation from the E. coli GRN data analysis.

claim: No E. coli or human TFs with in-degree >2 regulate TFs with out-degree >2.
source: Consistent with this idea, no E. coli or human TFs with in-degree >2 regulate TFs with out-degree >2 (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 3D.

claim: In S. cerevisiae there are several TFs that exceed the limits of in-degree >2 regulating TFs with out-degree >2, but this represents only a small minority of TFs.
source: In S. cerevisiae there are several TFs that exceed these limits, but this represents only a small minority of TFs (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3C.

claim: BQS strongly favours distributed control over central control.
source: These results show that BQS strongly favours distributed control over central control, and provide another example of BQS being a key determinant of the topology of GRNs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed properties of TF cross-regulation in GRNs.

claim: In the real GRNs of E. coli, S. cerevisiae and human, buffered motifs are much more abundant than would be expected by chance, while unbuffered motifs are much less abundant.
source: Figure 5A–F show that in the real GRNs of E. coli, S. cerevisiae and human, buffered motifs (blue) are much more abundant than would be expected by chance, while unbuffered (green and violet) motifs are much less abundant; and indeed, unbuffered motifs which are particularly susceptible to breaking BQS (violet) are rare.
evidence: This is supported by motif analysis shown in Figure 5A-F.

claim: Similar motif results hold for other confidence levels of E. coli, other confidence levels of S. cerevisiae, M. tuberculosis, P. aeruginosa, and other yeast datasets.
source: Similar results hold for other confidence levels of E. coli (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A–L), other confidence levels of S. cerevisiae (Figure 5—figure supplement 3M–X), M. tuberculosis (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B), P. aeruginosa (Figure 5—figure supplement 2,D), and other yeast datasets (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E–J).
evidence: This is supported by motif analysis shown in Figure 5 supplements.

claim: The prevalence of feedforward loops and bi-fans as building blocks of networks is explained by BQS.
source: These findings, besides confirming the role of BQS, provide additional support and potential explanations for the prevalence of well-studied motifs such as the feedforward loop (a stable motif) and the bi-fan (a buffered stable motif) as building blocks of networks (Alon, 2006; Milo et al., 2002).
evidence: This is an inference connecting BQS to previously observed network motifs, supported by citations.

claim: The most buffered 3- and 4-gene motifs are latent feed-forward loops and latent bi-fans, respectively.
source: Indeed, the most buffered 3- and 4-gene motifs studied here are, respectively, latent feed-forward loops and latent bi-fans.
evidence: This is an observation from the motif analysis.

claim: In the human GRN, 4363 new interactions can be added, but only 48 of them will create long feedback loops.
source: The extent of buffered stability is quite remarkable: 4363 new interactions can be added to the human GRN, but only 48 of them will create long feedback loops (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a result from computational analysis of the human GRN.

claim: Addition of single extra links to random networks would lead to the creation of approximately 2000 different feedback loops on average, with a hit rate of approximately 50%.
source: By contrast, addition of single extra links to random networks would lead to the creation of approximately 2000 different feedback loops on average: a hit rate of approximately 50%.
evidence: This is a result from computational simulations of random networks.

claim: The probability that real GRNs will gain long feedback loops by random edge additions is low and significantly smaller than that found for comparable random networks.
source: The probability that real GRNs will gain long feedback loops by random edge additions is low (Figure 5H, lightly shaded bars), and is significantly smaller than that found for comparable random networks (Figure 5H, heavily shaded bars).
evidence: This is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Of the seven 2-node feedback loops in the E. coli GRN, four are embedded into the two potentially unstable motifs depicted in Figure 6A,B, whilst the other three are isolated.
source: Firstly, of the seven 2-node feedback loops in the E. coli GRN, four are embedded into the two potentially unstable motifs depicted in Figure 6A,B, whilst the other three are isolated from other feedback loops and so are either stable or likely to act as switches.
evidence: This is an observation from the E. coli GRN data analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: The genes comprising the two illegal motifs in E. coli are involved in drug resistance and/or acid resistance.
source: Secondly, the genes comprising the two illegal motifs are involved in drug resistance (Ariza et al., 1995; Martin and Rosner, 2002; Nishino et al., 2008; Keseler et al., 2011; Figure 6C) and/or acid resistance (Sayed et al., 2007; Keseler et al., 2011; Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on gene function and data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Both illegal loops in E. coli share a remarkably similar sub-structure: two linked 2-gene feedback loops connected by one link into a 3-node feedback loop.
source: Thirdly, both loops share a remarkably similar sub-structure: two linked 2-gene feedback loops connected by one link into a 3-node feedback loop.
evidence: This is an observation from the E. coli GRN data analysis.

claim: A configuration of two linked 2-gene feedback loops connected by one link into a 3-node feedback loop can display chaotic behaviour in chemical networks.
source: It has been previously shown in chemical networks that such a configuration can display chaotic behaviour (Sensse and Eiswirth, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to work on chemical networks.

claim: Most of the genes in the illegal motifs in E. coli are highly regulated.
source: Moreover, compatible with the idea that chaotic behaviour should be tightly controlled, most of the genes depicted in Figure 6A,B are highly regulated (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: All four genes involved in the formation of illegal motifs in M. tuberculosis are implicated in stress responses.
source: These ideas are also supported by the M. tuberculosis GRN: all the four genes involved in the formation of illegal motifs are implicated in stress responses (He et al., 2006; Rodriguez et al., 2002), and the two 3-gene feedback loops share the same topology observed in E. coli (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on gene function and data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Of the six 2-node feedback loops observed in the M. tuberculosis GRN, three are isolated and the other three are embedded into the two potentially chaotic motifs.
source: In addition, of the six 2-node feedback loops observed in the M. tuberculosis GRN, three are isolated from other feedback loops and the other three are embedded into the two potentially chaotic motifs.
evidence: This is an observation from the M. tuberculosis GRN data analysis.

claim: The 4-gene feedback loop in the M. tuberculosis GRN is formed by joining the two 3-gene feedback loops.
source: Finally, it is noteworthy that the 4-gene feedback loop in the M. tuberculosis GRN is formed by joining the two 3-gene feedback loops (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C), consistent with our earlier observation that long feedback loops are susceptible to the formation of additional embedded feedback loops.
evidence: This is an observation from the M. tuberculosis GRN data analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: P. aeruginosa has no long (>3 genes) feedback loops.
source: P. aeruginosa has no long (>3 genes) feedback loops, and of its seven 2-node feedback loops five are isolated, and so are either stable or likely to act as switches, whilst the other two are linked but are of a form (positive-negative) that makes them Qualitatively Stable.
evidence: This is an observation from the P. aeruginosa GRN data analysis.

claim: Both of the S. cerevisiae 2-node feedback loops are isolated.
source: Both of the S. cerevisiae 2-node feedback loops are isolated, whilst the human GM12878 cell line has only a single 2-node feedback loop which is therefore isolated.
evidence: This is an observation from the S. cerevisiae GRN data analysis.

claim: The human GM12878 cell line has only a single 2-node feedback loop which is therefore isolated.
source: Both of the S. cerevisiae 2-node feedback loops are isolated, whilst the human GM12878 cell line has only a single 2-node feedback loop which is therefore isolated.
evidence: This is an observation from the human GM12878 GRN data analysis.

claim: The only long feedback loop observed in the yeast GRN derived by Lee et al. (2002) presents the same potentially chaotic topology as the illegal motifs in E. coli.
source: Curiously, the only long feedback loop observed in the yeast GRN derived by Lee et al. (2002) presents the same potentially chaotic topology discussed above.
evidence: This is an observation from the yeast GRN data analysis.

claim: The illegal motif observed in the yeast GRN derived by Lee et al. (2002) is not present in the more recent GRN derived by Harbison et al. (2004).
source: However, this illegal motif is not present in the more recent GRN derived by Harbison et al. (2004) (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an observation comparing two yeast GRN datasets, shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: The feedback loop distribution in the GRN of the leukaemia cell line K562 is strikingly different from that of the non-cancer cell line GM12878.
source: Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1 show that the feedback loop distribution in the GRN of the leukaemia cell line is strikingly different from that of the non-cancer cell line.
evidence: This is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: In K562, significantly more moderately long feedback loops of 4–8 genes are present compared to GM12878.
source: In K562, significantly more moderately long feedback loops of 4–8 genes are present (Figure 7A,B), and the number of loops formed by 3–5 genes is comparable to the number expected in a random network (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: The number of incomplete feedback loops is significantly larger in K562 compared to GM12878.
source: The number of incomplete feedback loops is also significantly larger in K562 (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 7C,D.

claim: Poorly buffered motifs are abundant in K562.
source: In addition, poorly buffered motifs are abundant (Figure 7E,F) and the TFs cross regulation is less extreme (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 7E,F and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Only a limited number of TFs contribute to the formation of the 59 long loops in the K562 GRN.
source: Interestingly, only a limited number of TFs contribute to the formation of the 59 long loops in the K562 GRN (Figure 7G) and it can be substantially 'stabilized'—that is most of the long feedback loops can be removed—by the removal of single pairs of TFs: FOSL1 and JUNB, JUNB and EGR1, or EGR1 and CEBPB.
evidence: This is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 7G.

claim: JUNB and FOSL1 are proto-oncogenes that are components of the AP-1 transcription complex.
source: JUNB and FOSL1 are proto-oncogenes that are components of the AP-1 transcription complex (Kouzarides and Ziff, 1989) and have been reported to be part of a long feedback loop in ovarian cancer (Stelniec-Klotz et al., 2012); EGR1 is a regulator of tumour suppressor genes and an oncogene itself (Baron et al., 2005); and the TFs of the C/EBP family have been described as both tumour promoters and suppressors (Nerlov, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on gene function.

claim: The three genes that contribute the most to the formation of long feedback loops in K562 (EGR1, FOSL1, and JUNB) are all involved in the formation of the longest incomplete feedback loops observed in GM12878.
source: We find that the three genes that contribute the most to the formation of long feedback loops in the cancer cell line (EGR1, FOSL1, and JUNB) are all involved in the formation of the longest incomplete feedback loops observed in the non-cancer cell line (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Of the 48 potentially destabilising interactions in GM12878, three are actually observed in K562: JUNB-BCLAF1, BATF-EBF1, and JUNB-EBF1.
source: Of these 48 potentially destabilising interactions of the non-cancer cell line, three are actually observed in the cancer cell line, namely JUNB-BCLAF1, BATF-EBF1, and JUNB-EBF1.
evidence: This is a result from computational analysis comparing GM12878 and K562 GRNs.

claim: The destabilizing interactions are five times more abundant in K562 than would be expected by chance.
source: Therefore, the destabilizing interactions are five times more abundant than would be expected by chance (0.063 vs 0.013), consistent with the idea that destabilizing interactions were positively selected for during the microevolution process underlying cancer progression.
evidence: This is a result from statistical analysis of the K562 GRN data.

claim: All the predictions of BQS are met in the murine dendritic cell GRN at 0 hr.
source: Figure 8 shows that all the predictions of BQS are met at this time.
evidence: This is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: The murine dendritic cell GRN at 0 hr has a very limited number of long feedback loops (only three with three or more genes).
source: As indicated by Figure 8A, the GRN has a very limited number of long feedback loops (only three with three or more genes), in striking contrast with the hundreds observed in randomly generated networks of the same link density.
evidence: This is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 8A.

claim: All of the long feedback loops in the murine dendritic cell GRN at 0 hr depend on the transcriptional interaction between SFPI1 and E2F1.
source: Interestingly, all of the long feedback loops depend on the transcriptional interaction between SFPI1 and E2F1 (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: E2F1 plays a crucial role in the cell cycle and is only transiently activated at commitment to cell division at the end of G1.
source: Notably E2F1 plays a crucial role in the cell cycle and is only transiently activated at commitment to cell division at the end of G1.
evidence: This is established knowledge about E2F1 function.

claim: The '0.5 hr' murine dendritic cell network still satisfies all the predictions of BQS and strongly resembles the '0 hr' network.
source: Indeed, the '0.5 hr' network still satisfies all the predictions of BQS and strongly resembles the '0 hr' network (Figure 9A,B,G).
evidence: This is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 9A,B,G.

claim: At 1 and 2 hr after the stimulus, a marked deviation from BQS is observed in murine dendritic cells.
source: In contrast, at 1 and 2 hr after the stimulus, a marked deviation from BQS is observed.
evidence: This is supported by data analysis of the murine dendritic cell GRN at different time points.

claim: A significant number of new long loops are created in murine dendritic cells at 1 hr after stimulus, peaking at 1 hr and declining slightly by 2 hr.
source: A significant number of new long loops are created, peaking at 1 hr and declining slightly by 2 hr (Figure 9C,E).
evidence: This is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 9C,E.

claim: 22 long feedback loops remain in murine dendritic cells at 2 hr after stimulus, but all depend on the transcriptional interaction between RUNX1 and CEBPB.
source: 22 long feedback loops remain at 2 hr, but interestingly all depend on the transcriptional interaction between RUNX1 and CEBPB.
evidence: This is a result from data analysis of the murine dendritic cell GRN at 2 hr.

claim: Some components of BQS remain unchanged in murine dendritic cells during stimulus response: incomplete feedback loops remain preferentially short, TF cross regulation remains essentially unchanged, and the numbers of unbuffered 3-node motifs and unregulated TFs remain low.
source: However, some components of BQS remain unchanged in the stimulus response. Incomplete feedback loops still remain preferentially short (Figure 9—figure supplement 1A,E,I), TF cross regulation remains essentially unchanged (Figure 9—figure supplement 1D,H,L) and the numbers of unbuffered 3-node motifs (Figure 9—figure supplement 1B,F,J) and unregulated TFs (Figure 9—figure supplement 1C,G,K) remain low.
evidence: This is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: BQS provides a theoretical justification for the ubiquitousness of network features already observed.
source: Besides leading to new predictions—that are consistently verified—BQS provides a theoretical justification for the ubiquitousness of network features already observed.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the contribution of BQS theory.

claim: BQS is an important step in providing a general mechanistic explanation for the overall structure of GRNs at different scales.
source: BQS is therefore an important step in providing a general mechanistic explanation for the overall structure of GRNs at different scales and in shedding new light on previous observations.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the contribution of BQS theory.

claim: The scarcity of feedback loops in E. coli has been remarked before, but the selective pressures underpinning this fact were not explored.
source: It is worth noting that the scarcity of feedback loops in E. coli has been remarked before (Shen-Orr et al., 2002), but the selective pressures underpinning this fact were not explored.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work and a statement about what was not done in that work.

claim: Defects in the GRN data are very unlikely to undermine the conclusions about BQS.
source: However, defects in the GRN data are very unlikely to undermine our conclusions, for various reasons.
evidence: This is followed by several arguments supporting this claim.

claim: Random networks with the same link density as the real GRNs do not satisfy BQS, whereas the real GRNs do.
source: First, as we have clearly shown, random networks with the same link density as the real GRNs do not satisfy BQS, whereas the real GRNs do.
evidence: This is supported by the data analyses comparing real and random networks throughout the manuscript.

claim: The compliance of real GRNs to BQS is essentially preserved when the rates of false positives and negatives are varied in the E. coli and S. cerevisiae GRN datasets.
source: Second, as illustrated thoroughly in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–J, Figure 3—figure supplement 3A,B, Figure 4—figure supplement 4A,B, and Figure 5—figure supplement 3A–X, the compliance of real GRNs to BQS is essentially preserved when the rates of false positives and negatives are varied in the E. coli and S. cerevisiae GRN datasets.
evidence: This is supported by sensitivity analyses shown in the cited figure supplements.

claim: The non-cancer (GM12878) and cancer (K562) cell lines show very different BQS properties, despite having similar link densities.
source: Third, the non-cancer (GM12878) and cancer (K562) cell lines show very different BQS properties, despite having similar link densities.
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis comparing GM12878 and K562 GRNs.

claim: BQS provides five simple rules for designing highly stable networks.
source: These principles are summarised by five simple rules (Figure 10): 1. Avoid long feedback loops to minimize instability arising from perturbations in network interactions (the basic principle of Qualitative Stability); 2. Favour constitutive (unregulated) nodes to reduce the potential number of loops; 3. Avoid long paths to minimize the number of 'incomplete feedback loops' and the emergence of instability due to addition of new network connections; 4. Favour buffered motifs over unbuffered motifs to reduce the potential number of loops; 5. Avoid centralized control hubs with a large number of both regulatory and regulating connections to reduce potential instability (necessitating the use of distributed control).
evidence: These rules are derived from the BQS theory and observations, and are illustrated in Figure 10.

claim: Motif analysis of post-transcriptional networks reveals that BQS-compliant feedforward loops are overrepresented, while BQS-breaking feedback loops are not.
source: However, the biological literature provides some clues. Motif analysis of post-transcriptional networks reveals that BQS-compliant feedforward loops are overrepresented, while BQS-breaking feedback loops are not (Gerstein et al., 2010; The modENCODE Consortium et al., 2010; Cheng et al., 2011; Joshi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on post-transcriptional networks.

claim: Stable motifs are more common than unstable ones even in post-transcriptional signal transduction.
source: Additionally, it has been noted that stable motifs are more common than unstable ones even in post-transcriptional signal transduction (Milo et al., 2002), suggesting again a role for Qualitative Stability in these networks.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work on signal transduction networks.

claim: The existence of feedback loops in post-transcriptional networks supports the idea that the severe constraints of BQS are 'loosened' to allow more responsive dynamic functionalities in post-transcriptional regulation.
source: Nevertheless, the existence of feedback loops in post-transcriptional networks (Harris and Levine, 2005; Tsang et al., 2007) supports the idea that the severe constraints of BQS are 'loosened' to allow more responsive dynamic functionalities in post-transcriptional regulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on citations to literature on post-transcriptional networks.

claim: Short feedback loops involving two or three genes appear to be present in some developmentally regulated gene networks.
source: Consistent with these expectations, short feedback loops involving two or three genes appear to be present in some developmentally regulated gene networks (Peter et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to literature on developmental gene networks.

claim: The different levels of gene regulation (transcriptional vs post-transcriptional) provide a way of segregating control modules with different robustness properties.
source: This raises the hypothesis that the different levels of gene regulation (transcriptional vs post-transcriptional) provide a way of segregating control modules with different robustness properties.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the observations about different levels of regulation.

claim: A certain level of instability builds up during a response to a stimulus that produces a transcriptional response in murine dendritic cells.
source: Consistent with this idea, our analysis indicates that a certain level of instability builds up during a response to a stimulus that produces a transcriptional response.
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis of murine dendritic cells at different time points after stimulus.

claim: Two hours after a stimulus, the murine dendritic cell GRNs are 'on the verge of stability', as the deactivation of just one transcriptional interaction will make the network robust according to the BQS rules.
source: Quite remarkably our results also suggest that two hours after such a stimulus the GRNs considered are 'on the verge of stability', as the deactivation of just one transcriptional interaction will make the network robust according to the BQS rules.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data analysis of murine dendritic cells at 2 hr after stimulus.

claim: The only instances where the E. coli and M. tuberculosis GRNs deviate from BQS are found in genes functionally related to stress responses.
source: It is notable that the only instances where the E. coli and M. tuberculosis GRNs deviate from BQS are found in genes functionally related to stress responses.
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis of illegal motifs in E. coli and M. tuberculosis GRNs.

claim: Therapeutic targeting of unstable motifs may provide a novel systems approach to drug discovery.
source: While other mechanisms are likely to be in play to achieve longer-term adaptations, therapeutic targeting of unstable motifs may provide a novel systems approach to drug discovery.
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion based on the findings about unstable motifs in stress response genes.

claim: The deviation of K562 from BQS allows a cancer cell to readily change its phenotype in response to internal or external stresses.
source: This deviation allows a cancer cell, in principle, to readily change its phenotype in response to internal or external stresses, so it can explore different phenotypic states, which might help its proliferation in otherwise challenging tissue environments, or even to survive drug treatment.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed deviation from BQS in K562.

claim: The cancer cell line K562 still possesses a degree of BQS far greater than that observed in a random network.
source: Nevertheless, the cancer cell line still possesses a degree of BQS far greater than that observed in a random network.
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis comparing K562 to random networks.

claim: Single-cell experiments report large changes in protein abundance occurring in individual cancer cells after drug treatment, consistent with the BQS theory.
source: We note that single-cell experiments report large changes in protein abundance occurring in individual cancer cells after drug treatment, consistent with our theory (Cohen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to experimental work on cancer cells.

claim: BQS adds a powerful new weapon to the arsenal of network medicine.
source: Taken together, our results indicate that BQS adds a powerful new weapon to the arsenal of network medicine (Barabasi et al., 2011; Noh et al., 2013; Pe'er and Hacohen, 2011).
evidence: This is a summary statement about the potential application of BQS, supported by citations to network medicine literature.

claim: The transcriptional interactions most critically involved in the formation of long feedback loops in K562 are also present in the longest incomplete feedback loops in GM12878.
source: The discovery that the transcriptional interactions most critically involved in the formation of long feedback loops in the cancer cell line K562 are also present in the longest incomplete feedback loops in the non-cancer cell line GM12878 may provide clues to mechanisms of cancer initiation and progression.
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis comparing K562 and GM12878 GRNs.

claim: Random perturbations to the GRN of normal cells will probably leave its stability unchanged.
source: Our theory suggests that random perturbations to the GRN of normal cells will probably leave its stability unchanged.
evidence: This is an inference based on the BQS theory and the observed properties of normal cell GRNs.

claim: Destabilization of the GRN is likely to involve those genes that are on the edge of stability, for example genes participating in long incomplete loops.
source: Destabilization of the GRN is likely to involve those genes that are on the edge of stability, for example genes participating in long incomplete loops.
evidence: This is an inference based on the BQS theory and the observed properties of GRNs.

claim: The two gene families with the highest destabilization potential in GM12878 (JUN and FOSL) are the two gene families with the highest destabilization role in K562.
source: It is striking that the two gene families with the highest destabilization potential in the non-cancer cell line (JUN and FOSL) are actually found to be the two gene families with the highest destabilization role in the cancer cell line.
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis comparing K562 and GM12878 GRNs.

claim: If network instability is a general feature of cancer cell GRNs, analysis of this kind can potentially be used to design new anti-cancer strategies.
source: If network instability is a general feature of cancer cell GRNs, analysis of this kind can potentially be used to design new anti-cancer strategies that exploit the unique weaknesses of cells lacking BQS.
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion about potential applications of BQS analysis.

claim: Condition 1 of Qualitative Stability (absence of positive self-regulation) is of questionable relevance to GRNs due to saturating effects on transcription and protein degradation.
source: For autocatalytic positive self-regulation, saturating effects on transcription (for example due to limiting numbers of RNA polymerases) along with protein degradation means that autocatalytic TFs will reach a stable steady-state rather than increasing to arbitrarily high values. Therefore condition 1 is of questionable relevance to GRNs.
evidence: This is an argument based on biological knowledge about transcription and protein dynamics.

claim: Condition 4 of Qualitative Stability (invertibility of the sign matrix) is trivially verified in GRNs.
source: GRNs breaking condition 4 have no biologically plausible incarnation. In order for this condition to be violated, two different TFs must act on the network in the same way, that is, they need to regulate each other and promote and inhibit exactly the same set of genes, as this would make the columns of the sign matrix linearly dependent and therefore the matrix non-invertible. If two TFs act in the way described, they would be biochemically indistinguishable. Due to the methodology used to derive GRNs, two such genes would be collapsed into the same node. Condition 4 is therefore trivially verified.
evidence: This is an argument based on the methodology of GRN construction and biological plausibility.

claim: Condition 3 (absence of feedback loops longer than two) is the most significant condition for Qualitative Stability in GRNs.
source: Taken together, the above considerations indicate that condition 3 is the most significant in a rigorous comparative study on the GRNs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analysis of the different conditions for Qualitative Stability in the context of GRNs.

claim: The E. coli RegulonDB dataset is probably the most validated GRN available in the literature.
source: The Escherichia coli RegulonDB dataset (Salgado et al., 2012) is probably the most validated GRN available in the literature.
evidence: This is a statement about the quality of the RegulonDB dataset, supported by a citation.

claim: The work by Harbison et al. (2004) is the most exhaustive yeast GRN derived from direct biological methods under stable conditions.
source: To the authors' knowledge, the work by Harbison et al. (2004) is the most exhaustive GRN derived from direct biological methods under stable conditions (rich media), and therefore the ideal workbench for a topological analysis.
evidence: This is a statement about the quality of the Harbison et al. dataset, supported by a citation.
